idiom_name: enum with associated values + exhaustive switch + failable factory
implementation_notes: A Swift enum is a closed set whose cases may carry associated values, which is exactly the variant set with per-case payloads; switch over an enum must be exhaustive or the code does not compile, so a new case is reported at every consumer. What replaces the sealed hierarchy is the enum itself: declare the cases with associated values, expose failable (init?) or throwing factories that validate, and use indirect enums when the model is recursive. Prefer enums over a struct holding an optional payload plus a tag: the enum has no illegal combination to represent, and Codable/Equatable can be synthesised for it.
code_sketch:
enum ConnectionState {
    case disconnected
    case connecting(initiated: Date)
    case connected(sessionID: String, lastPing: Date?)
}

switch state {                       // must be exhaustive
case .disconnected:
    print("down")
case .connecting(let initiated):
    print("connecting since \(initiated)")
case .connected(let sessionID, _):
    print(sessionID)
}
pitfalls: A default: clause silences the exhaustiveness error; also, a non-frozen enum from a library requires @unknown default, which deliberately trades the guarantee for forward compatibility.

Associated values are not Codable/Equatable/Hashable for free: Swift synthesises them only when every payload type does, and decoding untrusted JSON still needs validation in init(from:) or a factory.
Enums with associated values cannot have raw values, and pattern matching with if case can silently ignore other cases - keep a single exhaustive switch as the place where all variants are handled.
